questions.knowledge_point: Converting an Integral Over an Annular Region to Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/959705e66be54eff155f5e784f5a42c8fb5098b9fdf9ec877b794f196bd674bf.png)

The region $D$ in the fourth quadrant is enclosed between two quarter-circles centered at $O$ of radii $1$ and $2,$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

The region $D$ represents a portion of the washer enclosed between the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Region Enclosed Between Two Curves
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/ce35f6ef14576f536c268dd7420af6e0226609ab5305e85770f400439c2435de.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,.$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

- For $x=\frac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$  So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/f518a206638071a7b8548882a453123b6d78aed0aa94cc0e6e23429f22c6f1b3.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [r]_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting an Integral Over a Region Enclosed Between Two Curves to Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/15e58073c87bd249473950680a49e8fc4cb4be94277a7001c0ab9f96ab3a46df.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve $(x+2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ and the line $x=-3,$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(-2,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x+2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

- For $x=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-3 \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =-3 \\ r & =-\frac{3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =-3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the points $(-3,-\sqrt{3})$ and $(-3,\sqrt{3}).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{6}$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/928c6dc79f44a2185ccf217c0cf9210630b6554a698f805ef2c77500f9ddc76b.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,-3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le -4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{5\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{7\pi }{6}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{5\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}{\int }_{-3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{5\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{-3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/6ddc0b2138025b07ffdb7bf34afabeba578400b194922bec7a733cc9246c7c0f.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve $(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2$ and the line $y=2-x,$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at $(1,1).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =2 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)^{2} & =2 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2 & =2 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ r(r-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$

- For $y=2-x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2-x \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2 \\ r & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the points $(2,0)$ and $(0,2).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/587c299c1bdf89061be205cf185d6335fba865d2e30c81cac5b9d223fc84b486.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\le r\le 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ),\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2/(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{2/(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/636c9e587d6cbb9fcf9b24d068520330d5365cf80a2800bdd8244698512be3c0.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is enclosed between two circles centered at $O$ of radii $1$ and $5,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents the annulus between the disks of radii $1$ and $5$ centered at the origin. 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ we obtain $r=1.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25,$ we obtain $r=5.$

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})^{3/2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{{r}^{3}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[-\frac{1}{r}]}_{1}^{5}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1-\frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{5}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
